title: Good at many things
core: All three are compliments for not being one-dimensional, and all three imply a person (or thing) who can handle more than a single narrow demand. The confusion is that English praises breadth in at least three unrelated ways: by counting how many jobs you can do well, by counting how many sides you have, and by rating what you do when the normal means run out. One is a range-of-skill claim, one is a structural description, one is a behaviour-under-scarcity claim — and only the first is really about being "good at many things."
exam_note: The trap is **multifaceted**, which the exam attaches to problems, crises, and negotiations — things with no talents at all — while **resourceful** is signalled by a deprivation clause ("with no funding," "stranded"), not by breadth.

words.nuance: The only one that claims **demonstrated competence across separate domains** — you can be dropped into several different jobs and perform in each. It also travels comfortably to objects and materials (a versatile tool, a versatile stock), where the others either can't go or mean something else.

Counts **sides, not performances** — it describes the structure of something rather than crediting anyone with skill, which is why it fits a crisis, a career, or a policy debate as easily as a person. It's the flattering word for complexity: it tells you not to expect one cause or one label, and it's a favourite of citations and profile pieces.

Says nothing about how many skills you have; it rates **what you do when the resources aren't there** — no budget, no instructions, no obvious route. The praise carries an implied obstacle, so the word quietly reports that conditions were bad and the person refused to be stuck.
